why: Canary 1.1 took 2411 of 9785 requests (~24.6%, the expected 1-of-4-pod share) with 0 5xx and 0.00% error rate, identical to stable's 7374 requests / 0 5xx / 0.00%. Aggregate latency is equal or marginally better on the canary: p50 34 vs 34 ms, p95 93 vs 94 ms, p99 105 vs 104 ms. Per-route p50 and p95 match stable within 1-2 ms on all three routes (/browse 22/27 vs 22/27, /search 47/59 vs 47/59, /checkout 82/104 vs 81/103), so there is no route-specific regression hiding inside the aggregate. Two blemishes, stated explicitly: (1) canary /browse p99 is 77 ms vs stable 28 ms; (2) in the final 90-120s window canary p95 is 96 ms vs stable 92 ms, the only window where canary is worse (it was 92/92/93 vs 94/94/95 in the first three windows). Judgement: neither blemish is promote-blocking. The /browse p99 outlier sits below the canary's own overall p99 (105 ms) and below the /checkout p95 (104 ms), so it is tail noise on a 1200-request sample rather than a new slow path, and it does not move /browse p95 at all. The last-window gap is 4 ms with zero errors and no monotonic upward trend, which is within the window-to-window jitter already visible in stable's own series (92-95 ms). Judgement on residual risk: the canary only carried ~24.6% of load, so a contention-driven problem could still scale non-linearly at 100%; recommend promoting with latency/5xx alerts armed and keeping 1.0 ready for a fast rollback, and re-checking /browse p99 after the shift. On the evidence of zero errors and parity on p50/p95 across every route and every time window, blocking this release would be the unjustified call.
